World.title: One of Australia's iconic tropical islands now costs twice as much to run
World.content:
Tourism operators on the Great Barrier Reef are introducing passenger fuel surcharges and cutting services as soaring petrol costs put pressure on Australia's multi-billion-dollar tourism industry.

Tropical island resorts and large passenger boats powered by millions of litres of diesel each year are being pushed to the brink, according to the industry, with calls for COVID-era support for affected workers.

Association of Marine Park Tourism Operators (AMPTO) chief executive Gareth Phillips said operators in Cairns, Port Douglas and the Whitsundays were scaling back trips and cutting staff hours because they could not afford to run their boats.

"We're seeing reductions of 20 to 30 per cent in services," Mr Phillips said.

"Operators still need minimum crew levels for safety, but hours are being cut. That means less income, less certainty, and people starting to leave the industry."

CEO of the Australian Marine Park tourism Organisation Gareth Phillips wants passenger fees waived for the next six months. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

Mr Phillips said AMPTO had written to both the federal and Queensland governments, asking them to waive a range of per-passenger charges imposed on operators.

"There's been a lot of discussion, but not a lot of action," he said.

The Great Barrier Reef is a major drawcard for international tourists, injecting about $9 billion a year into the Australian economy, and employing 77,000 people, according to federal government figures.

Passengers travelling to the Great Barrier Reef are helping to cover the rising cost by paying surcharges. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

Mr Phillips said current conditions were tougher than the pandemic, when international border closures brought tourism to a halt.

"During COVID there was certainty and there was support," he said.

"Right now, it's the uncertainty around fuel pricing and availability that's alarming."

Tropical islands under pressure

On Green Island off Cairns, rising costs are filtering through the entire operation.

The coral cay is one of the most visited reef destinations in the country and has been welcoming tourists for more than a century.

While it has invested heavily in environmental management, including eco-tourism initiatives and wastewater treatment systems, the operation remains heavily exposed to fuel costs.

Green Island is one of the most visited reef destinations in the country. (Audience submitted: Seb Ian)

Solar power is used where possible, but dense canopy limits output, meaning most of the island's energy still comes from diesel generators — powering accommodation, kitchens, air-conditioning and essential services.

Quicksilver Group CEO Tony Baker said the company used 300,000 litres of fuel a month across its operations.

"From late February through to the first week of the Easter school holidays, our fuel costs went up 168 per cent," he said.

Quicksilver CEO Tony Baker said fuel costs are hitting reef operators hard. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

Those costs are now being passed on to visitors through fuel surcharges, but Mr Baker said the increase still did not cover total operating costs.

"It's not something we want to do — and it's not something customers want — but sometimes it's necessary," he said.

But he said the bigger issue was unpredictability.

Green Island Resort off Cairns recycles human waste in a bid to cut down on its carbon footprint. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

"Prices are changing week to week, and that makes it very hard when fuel is such a big cost," he said.

"If we don't get minimum numbers to cover the cost of that vessel, we won't operate."

'If we don't get the numbers … we won't fly'

Rising fuel costs are also forcing the skydiving industry to rethink how it flies — and how often.

Skydive Australia's Regional Operations Manager for North Queensland, Paul Poulos, said about 20 staff were needed to accommodate between 1,000 and 2,000 jumps a month, depending on weather conditions.

"We're certainly seeing pressure from rising fuel costs," Mr Poulos said.

Skydive Australia's regional operations manager for North Queensland, Paul Poulos, says the industry is feeling the pressure. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

"That's across aircraft operations, transport and logistics. It flows through everything we do."

While the cost of jumps has held steady for now, he said the focus had shifted to keeping aircraft full and matching schedules to demand.

"We're looking at maximising loads, matching staffing to demand and consolidating operating days where we can," he said.

Track the latest petrol and diesel prices around Australia See what's happening with petrol and diesel prices near you, updated constantly.

"If we don't get the numbers to make a flight viable, we won't fly it."

He said it was important to maintain skydiving experiences in regional tourism hubs like Cairns and Airlie Beach.

"These are iconic destinations. People build their holidays around them," he said.

"And if we lose accessibility, it doesn't just impact us, it impacts the whole region."

Calls for help

Across Australia, regional tourism businesses reported a subdued Easter holiday period, largely driven by rising fuel prices affecting road trips.

Australian Regional Tourism CEO Lauren Douglass said the industry was "in crisis" and bookings from May onwards were "almost non-existent".

"Demand is weakening in regions more than two hours from capital cities, with bookings down by up to 40 per cent in some areas," Ms Douglass said.

Federal Opposition tourism spokesman David Littleproud said he had written to Tourism Minister Don Farrell calling for a COVID-era response to support regional tourism operators including grants.

"Regional tourism relies on travellers feeling confident to hit the road, to fuel up, and to explore Australia's vast interior. When the government runs campaigns that frame fuel use as something to be avoided or reduced, it sends a message to prospective travellers," Mr Littleproud said.

A federal government spokesman said it was "co-ordinating closely with state and territory governments, and taking every practical step to shield Australians from the worst impacts of the conflict in the Middle East".

World.title: Health insurer Bupa accused of anti-competitive behaviour
World.content:
Health insurance giant Bupa has been accused of anti-competitive behaviour in its dealings with private hospitals, which critics say is ultimately reducing choice for Bupa customers.

Leaked documents have revealed how the insurer's contracts impose stifling conditions on small hospitals — operators with little bargaining power against a fund that holds a quarter of the Australian market.

Particular concern centres on Bupa's Medical Gap Scheme, with private hospitals saying the insurer uses the terms of its hospital agreements to prevent its subcontracted doctors charging patients any out-of-pocket costs.

Former Bupa executive David Du Plessis, who now works as a contracts consultant for private hospitals, has backed the claims.

He said the complex nature of billing meant hospitals that refused to sign a contract left their doctors facing a stark choice — either accept lower payments from the insurer per procedure or pass significant out-of-pocket costs onto their patients.

"It is a wedge. It's a way of forcing the hospital, who have to hold the contract," he said.

While avoiding any out-of-pockets may sound good for patients, David du Plessis warned they could lose out too.

Doctors are unable to use Bupa's Medical Gap Scheme at a non-contracted hospital, meaning patients who go to one of those 99 facilities can face a double hit: out-of-pocket costs from both the hospital and the doctor.

"They're removing choice from their members," Mr du Plessis told ABC News.

"What Bupa is really in effect doing with this is saying: 'Well, you can choose your specialist, but you're going to bear a lot of costs with that specialist unless they go to a hospital that we hold a contract with.'

" It's the consumer in the end that's also wearing the cost of this to the benefit of Bupa and its profitability. "

Bupa said in a statement the claims about its gap scheme were baseless and the scheme was designed "to help customers pay less, and in many cases nothing, for medical out-of-pocket costs".

What is the Bupa gap scheme?

Bupa's Medical Gap Scheme has been operating in its current form since 2021.

It is applied when patients are treated as a "No Gap" or "Known Gap" patient in a private hospital, which means they should only pay their excess — or up to $500 on top of that if they are a Known Gap patient.

Documents show the long arms of Bupa's contracts with some hospitals. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Typically, under contracts with hospitals, an insurer details what it will pay the hospital for theatre and room fees if customers are treated as a no-medical-gap or fixed-fee patient.

It is then up to doctors whether they will apply No Gap schemes on their share of the procedure.

The two can decide independently of each other whether to apply a No Gap bill.

However, Bupa's Medical Gap Scheme operates differently, by using the terms of the hospital contracts to stipulate that physicians cannot charge a gap fee either.

It also means Bupa No Gap doctors cannot make use of the scheme at uncontracted hospitals.

This ultimately forces Bupa customers to use a Bupa-contracted hospital if they want no out-of-pocket expenses on their procedure, as well as the hospital stay.

"For those patients unaware of the Bupa deals, if they end up in an uncontracted hospital for a major procedure … they could be looking at thousands in out-of-pockets," Mr du Plessis said.

Jane Griffiths, who is the chief executive of Day Hospitals Australia, said the doctors were subcontractors and the terms were unfair.

"It's basically making the hospital the policeman for the doctor's fees. This is the only insurer that does that," she said.

Jane Griffiths says Bupa's Medical Gap Scheme is different to other insurers. (ABC News: West Matteeussen)

Mr du Plessis warned that if doctors earned less because the hospital was off-contract, they would likely leave the hospital.

"That's a huge disadvantage for hospitals," he said.

That ultimately forced the hospital to enter a contract, even when the prices proposed were unsustainable.

"It comes down to that moral question of whether or not you should or shouldn't be doing this," Mr du Plessis said.

A Bupa spokesperson said the scheme aimed to help customers avoid unexpected bills "and get the care they need with confidence".

Uncontracted hospitals in Bupa's sights

The ABC can reveal that, since August last year, Bupa has also been trying to impose a similar condition on doctors at uncontracted hospitals.

In a letter to the Australian Society of Ophthalmologists, Bupa stated its specialists could start using the No Gap scheme for doctors' fees at some of the 99 hospitals across the country it did not have a contract with.

But, it stipulated they could only do so, "provided they [the uncontracted hospital] give and continue to comply with a written undertaking not to charge Bupa customers any out-of-pocket costs beyond the applicable excess…"

Australian Private Hospitals Association chief executive Brett Heffernan described it as "beyond the pale".

"They're squeezing the hospital on one end in terms of the contract negotiation and they're squeezing the doctors on the other end to put pressure onto the hospitals to capitulate," he said.

The association has called on the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) to act, alleging it is anti-competitive behaviour.

"This is a situation where Bupa are trying to have the hospital over a barrel and dictate pricing. It's completely inappropriate," Mr Heffernan said.

While Bupa argues its gap scheme is about benefiting patients, APRA data shows Bupa's benefits-ratio payment, which is the percentage of incoming premiums it pays out to members as benefits, is 82.4 per cent.

This compares to competitors such as Medibank Private at 85.6 per cent and HCF at 87.8 per cent.

"So for Bupa to be at 83 per cent, they are a long, long way behind where they need to be in fulfilling their obligations to their members," Mr Heffernan argued.

Terms could be anti-competitive

Bashi Hazard says Bupa's Medical Gap Scheme could be an example of the anti-competitive vertical restraint. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Bashi Hazard lectures in competition law at the University of Sydney's Law School. She said the gap scheme could be anti-competitive if it was found to be both coercive and limiting competition in small areas.

"What we're looking at in this situation could be a vertical restraint," Dr Hazard said.

"That is something that, particularly in regional areas, the regulator would have to take a close look at."

What is No Gap and Known Gap cover? No gap cover: Patients receive no out-of-pocket charges for their treatment for doctor fees. Insurers pay a higher rate per procedure than Medicare's Schedule Fee to doctors to encourage uptake. Known gap cover: Patients will be charged a fixed out-of-pocket amount for their treatment by a doctor, up to a maximum of $500 for general treatment and $800 for obstetrics. Out-of-pocket charges: Patients not using No Gap or Known Gap cover can face out-of-pocket costs. This is the difference between the overall cost of the procedure and the usual combined Medicare and insurer general rebates. Agreement or network hospitals: The agreements between hospitals and insurers relating to the room, nursing and theatre fees. Sometimes they also result in fixed fee arrangements similar to known gaps. Source: Department of Health and Aged Care.

Bupa said in a statement it had previously contacted some non-contracted hospitals to outline "voluntary contracting options" that could support lower out-of-pocket costs for members.

"Doctors were never asked to ensure hospital fees were waived, and any arrangements are optional, case by case, and focused on improving affordability for patients," a spokesperson said.

They said hospitals were free to negotiate with other insurers, which could help promote competition.

"[For uncontracted hospitals], we don't set doctors' fees or hospitals' charges, nor do we ask doctors to influence hospital fees," they said.

" Ultimately our approach will benefit the entire sector as it encourages greater participation, choice and transparency. "

Power of Bupa's market share

Bupa is one of Australia's largest health insurers, with nearly 4 million customers nationally and a quarter of the market, so it is seen as essential for most hospitals to contract with the insurer.

It is the market leader in South Australia with more than 40 per cent market share.

It reported a full-year after-tax profit of $594 million in 2024–25, higher than any other private health insurer.

"In states where Bupa has a huge market share, it becomes doubly problematic," Mr du Plessis said.

A Bupa spokesperson said patients in regional areas could have fewer choices, and "that's why we work closely with our customers to ensure they have access to care at any of our contracted hospitals".

Small hospitals feeling the brunt

Mr du Plessis said he found what compounded the problem for many small hospitals was that Bupa was slow to even offer contracts, especially to new hospitals.

"I'm seeing a number of providers citing difficulties with getting contracts, with Bupa in particular, particularly new hospitals that are opening, and being able to then establish reasonable rates with them," he said.

" They've had significant delays through the negotiation. They'll send an email to try and continue the next step of a negotiation and may not even receive a response for weeks. "

When he worked at Bupa, they had about six staff to negotiate with more than 600 private hospitals and he said sometimes delays were part of the strategy.

The contracts obtained by the ABC showed the long arms of these contracts.

Hospitals must get permission from the insurer if they intend to open a new unit or wing, show evidence of why it is needed, the names of the doctors involved, how they will attract patients and even guess how many Bupa patients might use it if they want to get their higher contracted rates.

While legally it is allowed, the Australian Private Hospitals Association said it was onerous and broke the compact with customers to only insure for services, not direct them.

Mr du Plessis said the business rules hampered flexibility for even big hospital groups.

Brett Heffernan says moves by Bupa are "beyond the pale". (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Mr Heffernan said secrecy provisions in contracts prevented anyone objecting publicly.

"We see clauses in there about what hospitals can and can't do, and one of the things they can't do is talk to anybody about what the egregious terms of these contracts are," he said.

Bupa said its contracting practices complied with competition law and "operated under regulatory oversight".

Peak body Private Healthcare Australia, which represents health insurers, said No Gap arrangements were designed to avoid surprise medical bills.

"People with private health cover consistently tell us they want certainty about what treatment will cost. No Gap arrangements are designed to provide that certainty," chief executive Rachel David said.

*In this story "No Gap" refers to both No Gap and Known Gap charging.

World.title: Casualty list from AI bubble moves up a gear as Apple's Tim Cook exits
World.content:
His departure, seemingly without warning, stunned the world. But Tim Cook's time had come, cut short by his perceived unwillingness to confront a technological shift that now has swallowed him.

For a man who helped usher in Apple's communications revolution, it was the ultimate irony.

More than 1.5 billion people across the planet feel completely dependent on the technology he pioneered and, if not quite physically attached, consider their iPhone to be an essential part of everyday life.

Add in another billion or so Apple products out there, from Macs to iPads, AirPods, and even the odd remaining iPod, and it's little wonder the devotion many consumers had to the products was embraced in equal measure by shareholders.

His replacement by long-time Apple executive John Ternus marks a turning point for the company with profound implications for global investors, including our very own superannuation giants.

John Ternus will become Apple's next chief executive officer on September 1. (Reuters: File)

Apple has been a key contributor to the incredible growth in Australian retirement savings, particularly since the global financial crisis.

The numbers tell the story.

Under Cook's 14-year reign, Apple's market valuation soared from $US350 billion ($488 billion) to more than $US4 trillion ($5.6 trillion). Revenue quadrupled to $US416 billion ($580 billion).

But at some point, in the past few years, Cook was left behind.

A cautious and thoughtful man who prioritised user privacy, a once winning combination that helped catapult Apple into global corporate dominance, Cook's approach was perceived as a dragging anchor in the race for artificial intelligence (AI) domination

Apple has always had an insular approach. It forged its own pathway, developing technology and even its own chips in-house. Its hardware outlasted the opposition.

But around this time last year, investors began asking questions. Why was Cook underspending on AI development, especially considering the frenzied activity of his competitors?

And why was he content to let Siri, the AI application first introduced by Apple back in 2010, languish?

Apple scruffs

Cook may well turn out to have made the right choice.

At the beginning of this year, Apple's main competitors — Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft — pledged to outlay a combined $US650 billion in capital expenditure, most of which will be directed to AI.

The thinking within Apple, or at least by Cook, was that AI would become a mere commodity to be bought and sold.

Cook hooked Apple up with long-time nemesis Google to provide AI technology for Siri for what is believed to be about $US1 billion ($1.4 billion), a mere fraction of Google's AI outlay and a pittance when compared to the industry splurge.

Google has invested heavily in AI technology. (Getty: Alain Jocard)

But for many, that financially conservative approach threatened to undermine the very essence of Apple's existence; its independence.

Google technology powers Android phones. There were fears that allowing the rival to power a key segment of its own platform, the intelligence side, may sideline Apple into merely providing hardware.

As concerns mounted midway through last year, Apple shares were slammed before a Christmas recovery. This year, they've flatlined.

On an annual basis, Apple delivered a 29 per cent return, which doesn't sound unreasonable. But it pales in comparison with Google parent Alphabet, which delivered 114 per cent growth.

Is your money putting you out of work?

There's a lot riding on Cook's replacement, John Ternus, a man who has been involved in every major product release since he joined in 2001.

Australian investors have about $9 billion invested in the company through our major superannuation funds. Australian Super accounts for about one-third of that.

Like many global investors, a large chunk of Australia's $4 trillion super pot has been directed towards AI and the handful of US corporations that dominate the sphere.

Australians' super savings exposed as clouds gather over tech boom Amongst tech investors the penny has finally dropped about just what the future may hold, and many are backing off or at least rethinking their strategy.

The most recent estimates are that Australian exposure to artificial investment firms totals about $140 billion, but the recent resurgence on Wall Street, driven in large part by a recovery in some of the biggest tech firms, undoubtedly would have lifted that.

In the past week, competition among the tech giants continued, despite the well-aired concerns the whole thing resembles an enormous financial bubble.

Amazon tipped $US5 billion ($7 billion) into AI's rising star, Anthropic. That was on top of the $US8 billion ($11.1 billion) already committed, hinting there was $US20 billion ($28 billion) more to come.

Anthropic, in turn, agreed to spend more than $US100 billion ($140 billion) on Amazon's cloud services over the next decade.

Then, over the weekend, Google stumped up $US10 billion ($14 billion) for Anthropic with another $US30 billion ($42 billion) on offer, strengthening an already close relationship.

Meanwhile, the race to build data centres shows no sign of abating.

Despite the imminent threat of a global energy crisis, there is no shortage of cash being thrown at AI infrastructure firms and the data centres that consume vast quantities of electricity and water.

Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella strutted the stage in Sydney last week, announcing plans to fork out $25 billion over the next three years for a series of data centres on the world's driest continent.

He'll be jostling for space from local contenders like NextDC, Firmus and AirTrunk.

Many companies are building data centres in Australia. (Supplied: Microsoft)

Xi and Trump have something in common

Tim Cook wasn't the only one in the tech world to find himself at a loose end last week.

Both Facebook parent Meta and Microsoft announced global lay-offs that could cut as many as 23,000 staff, adding to an already extensive list of casualties in the past year.

Loading...

Legitimate fears that AI could kill far more jobs than it creates appear to be reinforced as the architects behind the revolution have been among the first affected.

Even in China, an unexpected surge in unemployment numbers last week, particularly among younger workers, pointed to the sudden arrival of AI.

Youth unemployment in the Middle Kingdom, where official statistics often tend to gloss over economic trends, rose strongly and ticked up to 7.7 per cent for those aged 25 to 29, a record high.

Citi economists believe this could create concerns within Beijing.

Oil shock, federal budget and recession we may have to have Even with optimistic NDIS savings locked in, the Strait of Hormuz complicates Australia’s economic forecasts — and risks rendering the 2026 budget largely irrelevant.

"The unexpected deterioration for early career workers, who are more likely AI exposed, seems to point to the unfolding AI-driven replacement and we believe the structural headwinds from AI adoption are set to identify," they wrote in a note to clients.

"We remain cautious on the labour market and consumption outlook and see the mid-year Politburo as a plausible venue for policy adjustment."

Meanwhile, in the US, President Donald Trump is facing his own AI problems.

The multi-billion-dollar rush to build data centres may have bolstered US economic growth figures, masking the impact of his tariff policies.

But the shortage of high technology materials needed for their construction has lit a fire under imports, worsening America's massive trade deficit.

As his struggle to bring the Iran war to an end goes on, gasoline prices continue to escalate. And now his long-promised fix to the US trade deficit is becoming increasingly out of reach.

World.title: The security breach that exposed Trump to a gunman
World.content:
The shots rang out just after dinner began, when Donald Trump, JD Vance and other senior US officials were chatting on a dais in the ballroom of the Washington Hilton hotel.

One level above, secret agents were hot on the tail of a man armed with a shotgun, a handgun and knives, who had just breached a security checkpoint.

He dashed though a hallway, passed a set of elevators and made it to the anteroom where hundreds of Washington's most high-profile politicians, diplomats and journalists had stood hours earlier.

A digital rendering of the Washington Hilton floor plan. (ABC News/Supplied)

Inside the ballroom, a team raced towards Mr Trump and the first lady to escort them and other VIPs to safety.

Everyone else quickly ducked under tables, while journalists pulled out their phones to try to make sense of the commotion unfolding before them.

Guests take cover as Secret Service agents rush the president and vice-president from the White House Correspondent's Association dinner. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

Members of the Secret Service moved in as the suspect headed toward a set of stairs that would have taken him to the room where guests had been served a spring pea and burrata salad.

He was tackled face-first into the carpet and put in handcuffs.

The alleged gunman has since been identified as 31-year-old Cole Tomas Allen.

US President Donald Trump posted a picture of the suspected shooter on social media. (Truth Social: @realDonaldTrump)

"It does appear that [the shooter] did, in fact … set out to target folks that work in the administration, likely including the president," Todd Blanche, the acting attorney-general, told NBC's Meet the Press program.

The incident has sparked memories of the assassination attempt on Mr Trump at an outdoor rally in Butler, Pennsylvania in 2024.

Two months later he was again the target of a would-be assassin as he played a round on his Florida golf course.

The correspondents' dinner was his first as president — Mr Trump boycotted the event during his first term in office.

"That was very unexpected," he said in a press conference hours afterwards, still in his tuxedo.

A Secret Service officer was shot but was "saved" by his bulletproof vest, according to Mr Trump. No-one was seriously injured.

In the aftermath of the chaotic event, the Secret Service quickly moved to lock down the hotel and the dinner was postponed.

Mr Blanche reassured viewers on Sunday that while the shooting was "extraordinarily dangerous and put a lot of lives at risk", the security "system worked".

But that sentiment was not shared by everyone in attendance.

Trump dinner shooting live updates: For the latest news on the White House Correspondents' Association dinner shooting, read our blog.

"Started as a great night — though we noticed security was nearly non-existent," Kari Lake, a former Republican Senate nominee in Arizona and senior adviser for the US Agency for Global Media, said on X.

The incident has now raised questions about the level of security around the US president and how a shooter was able to breach a checkpoint and get so close to the country's most senior leadership.

Trump and Vance pulled from room in 'different directions'

The annual gala, in which the White House press mingles with the president and other high-profile officials, was hosted as always by the Hilton.

The 60-year-old hotel in Washington's Dupont Circle neighbourhood sits less than 3 kilometres away from the White House and has been the scene of violence in the past.

It was the site of an attempted assassination that left then-president Ronald Reagan seriously wounded in 1981.

Loading...

Mr Reagan had been outside the building, walking toward his limousine after a labour meeting, when he was shot in the rib and rushed to hospital. It took two hours of surgery to remove the .22 calibre bullet, which had pierced his lung.

In the aftermath of that shooting, the Secret Service added a garage to the hotel, so that limousines carrying the president and vice-president could pull in without being visible to anyone outside the hotel.

This time, however, the danger lurked inside.

Videos circulating online show Secret Service agents responded to the intruder threat by grabbing the US president, the first lady and the vice-president from their seats within seconds.

How dinner with the president descended into chaos Thousands of influential players in Washington filed into a ballroom with the US president. Then shots rang out.

"I think the detail of each of the president and vice-president responded quickly, efficiently," former Secret Service agent Robert McDonald told ABC NewsRadio.

"You'll notice that, if you watch the film, both of those individuals were taken off the stage in different directions. You don't want people crossing ways."

Mr Vance's detail was quicker to get him out, with the president falling down as he was escorted by security.

Mr Trump later said he believed he might have caused the minor delay in exiting the room.

"Well, what happened is, it was a little bit me," Mr Trump said in an interview on CBS's 60 Minutes.

"I wanted to see what was happening and I wasn't making it easy for them. I wanted to see what was going on."

The measures in place

The Hilton does not close to other guests when it hosts the correspondents' dinner, but access to the event is restricted.

"The Secret Service, in a situation like a hotel, in a ballroom, does not like to shut down the entire hotel based upon a separate event that might be going on there," Mr McDonald said.

Security is focused on the ballroom where the correspondents' dinner is held, rather than the broader hotel, which contains more than 1,100 guest rooms and suites as well as 47 meeting rooms.

"I think that this is probably going to be looked at by the Secret Service, to see how to enhance situations like this where there is a side of the venue that is remaining open for regular business," Mr McDonald said.

In the past, protesters have caused disruptions in the lobby and other public spaces around the hotel.

This year, guests of the hotel and event attendees were able to pass through checkpoints in surrounding streets by simply showing a copy of their dinner ticket.

ABC reporter at Trump dinner when shots rang out ABC Americas editor was inside the ballroom when a shooting suspect was stopped by the Secret Service.

The ABC's Americas editor, John Lyons, was one of many journalists in attendance and said all he needed to get in was a ticket, which did not have a name on it.

Ms Lake also said on social media that "nobody asked to visibly INSPECT my ticket nor asked for my photo identification" when she entered the venue.

"All one had to do was flash what appeared to be a ticket and they were fine with that," she wrote.

"…You would think they would have better security."

It was Senator John Fetterman's view, that the venue "wasn't built to accommodate an event with the line of succession for the US government".

He was referring to how five of the top six officials in line to the US presidency attended the event.

"I can't remember a president that had as many cabinet members in and around him and at events and at venues or at press conferences as this president," Mr McDonald, who worked with the Secret Service for over 20 years, said.

"It's very similar to our State of the Union or an inauguration where when you have all of those people in one area, that's not a good look for somebody who wants to commit some nefarious activity."

NBC reported that the White House Correspondents' Association dinner was not designated a National Special Security Event, a classification used for nationally significant events like presidential inaugurations, presidential nominating conventions and major sporting events.

Designated events are granted by the Department of Homeland Security and can receive federal funding for additional security.

When approached for comment, a Secret Service spokesperson told the ABC it did not make these designations.

Along with Secret Service agents and other law enforcement who formed part of the security apparatus inside the hotel, some American news outlets, including Fox News and CNN, also brought security detail inside the ballroom with attendees, according to the Wall Street Journal.

CNN's head security officer reportedly climbed over chairs to get to chief executive Mark Thompson and chief White House correspondent and anchor Kaitlin Collins, to protect them after shots rang out.

The security breach inside

US Attorney-General Todd Blanche said the alleged gunman travelled by train from Los Angeles to Chicago and then on to Washington before the shooting.

The man checked into a room at the same venue as the Washington dinner one or two days before the incident in the ballroom.

"We believe that the two firearms he had on him, he had purchased within the past couple of years," Mr Blanche said.

Authorities did not think anybody else was involved in the incident on Saturday.

It's likely the alleged gunman walked right through the front lobby, Mr McDonald said, since it was "not secured for this event".

Shattered glass near the ballroom at the Washington Hilton hotel. (Reuters: Kylie Cooper)

He said while a person should declare if they are carrying weapons in a hotel when checking in, there is no mandate for them to do so.

"I don't believe that there's any law or policy here that requires that," he said.

Mr McDonald added he was not sure the Secret Service was sweeping every single room in the hotel "because of the distance it is from the ballroom".

Guests and visitors could access the Hilton's lobby and lower levels on the night of the event and they only had to pass through one checkpoint that was set up on the terrace level, one floor above the ballroom.

From there, attendees took a set of stairs to the international ballroom, where the function was held. It sits on the concourse level, two floors below the hotel's main entrance and lobby.

The alleged gunman wrote in a 1,052-word manifesto before the attack at the Hilton that he expected "security cameras at every bend, bugged hotel rooms and armed agents every 10 feet, metal detectors out the wazoo".

Who is Donald Trump's would-be assassin? Details from the life of US President Donald Trump's would-be assassin paint a picture of a high achiever who took an abrupt turn towards political violence.

The alleged writings were published by the New York Post and have not been independently verified by the ABC.

"What I got (who knows maybe they are pranking me!) is nothing," the suspect wrote in an apparent manifesto.

"I walk in with multiple weapons and not a single person there considers the possibility that I could be a threat," he added.

But when Mr Blanche was asked if he believed that law enforcement met all the standards for an event of that magnitude, he replied "absolutely. 100 per cent."

"You cannot stop living, you cannot stop being in public … and so how do you create an environment that keeps people safe but still allows them to live in this great country, and to walk around, and to have a dinner?" he told Meet the Press.

Trump says this is why 'we need the ballroom'

Despite Mr Trump being happy with how Secret Service responded on Saturday night, there are many questions that remain unanswered on how an event of this scale could have such a security blunder.

The president has used the opportunity to promote his controversial White House ballroom.

Donald Trump addressing media after the shooting incident. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

"We need the ballroom. That's why Secret Service … the military are demanding it," Mr Trump said, without offering evidence that presidential security officials have issued such demands.

Mr McDonald said he thought based upon what he saw and the need for a large venue, the president "has a point".

"I think he's probably going to use that point to run with the continued building of that ballroom on the east side of the White House," he said.

A review of the incident by FBI's criminal investigation and terrorism taskforce is underway.

"I think in the recent or the near future, we're going to see a tightness around the president," Mr McDonald said.

He said that was likely to be the case given King Charles III and Queen Camilla's state visit to the United States.

"I think you are going to see a very strong, very robust security element in and around his visit here," Mr McDonald said.

The royal visitors already face a diplomatic challenge to resolve political tensions between the US and the UK since the start of the war in Iran.

Now, there is an added layer of security concerns to the existing complexities.

World.title: Search for missing 5yo enters third day as helicopters, heat drones deployed
World.content:
Three days since Sharon Granites disappeared from an Alice Springs town camp, police are continuing to cover a vast area of land with helicopters, horses and drones as they search for some signs of the five-year-old.

Sharon went missing at around 11:30pm on Saturday, with Northern Territory Police on Monday saying they believe she has been abducted by a recently released prisoner, 47-year-old Jefferson Lewis.

Five-year-old Sharon Granites has been missing for more than two days. (Supplied: NT Police Force)

Mr Lewis was recently released from prison after serving an 18-month sentence for serious violence-related offences, and is now also the subject of the wide-scale police manhunt.

The search began late on Saturday night, after Sharon's family realised she had gone missing from her home in the Old Timers camp — a house in which police confirmed Mr Lewis was also staying.

Members of the community starting conducting searches for Sharon, but were unable to find her.

Sharon Granites was noticed missing from her home at the Old Timers town camp at about 11:30pm on Saturday. (ABC News: Will Green)

In the early hours of Sunday morning, when police were alerted to her disappearance, doorknocks and further searches by officers were conducted in and around the community.

Over Sunday and Monday, the air search for Sharon covered around 46 square kilometres, while the foot search area has encompassed around 20 square kilometres, much of which is covered by thick scrubland and rough terrain.

Ilyperenye/Old Timers town camp is situated between the Alice Springs town centre and the suburb of Kilgariff. (ABC News Graphics: Jessica Henderson)

As well as two helicopters, the search for Sharon has used heat sensor drones and dozens of emergency services and non-government organisation workers joining forces for ground searches.

Sergeant Matt Hall said the search had so far been "slow going" due to the environment.

Police and volunteers have been conducting on-foot line searches for Sharon Granites. (ABC News: Will Green)

"It is a vast search area that we are looking at and going through methodically," he told ABC Radio Darwin.

"The area's heavily overgrown with buffel grass, so in some areas it's shoulder-to-shoulder search pattern through that area.

" So, it is slow going, but we will continue to push through. "

Parts of the foot search area are overgrown with buffel grass, making the search "slow going". (ABC News: Will Green)

Town camp organisation assisting in searches

As well as NT Police, NT Fire and Rescue has been assisting in the searches, as well as Alice Springs-based organisations including Tangentyere Council and Purple House.

Tangentyere Council president Maxine Carlton said about 36 of their staff had taken part in foot patrols.

Maxine Carlton says dozens of Tangentyere Council staff are helping with the searches. (ABC News: Will Green)

"We've also reached out to other Aboriginal organisations to assist in this search," she said.

" We came onboard straight away as we knew, this is a town camp, we are a part of this. "

Tangentyere Council is also helping to support Sharon's family and other Old Timers community members as they deal with the stress and trauma of the circumstances.

Alice Springs-based organisations have been rallying to help the search effort. (ABC News: Will Green)

"This is a very distressing time for all families," Ms Carlton said.

She said that while police had been doing exceptional work in the search, the wider community should have been notified "within an hour" after Sharon went missing.

"Alice Springs should've been in a lockdown [by Sunday morning]," she said.

"But we would like to thank the police, and the SES, they doing a really fantastic job.

Maxine Carlton hopes the search will deliver "good news" soon. (ABC News: Will Green)

"We hope there's good news in the near future."

Sergeant Hall said the wider Alice Springs community could help by keeping their eyes open.

"The biggest thing the community can do at this stage is [be the] eyes and ears," he said.

"Anything they see, anything they hear, no matter how minor they think it might be, it could be that relevant small bit of information which could … lead us to successfully locating young Sharon."

World.title: The best ways to protect credit and debit cards from fraud
World.content:
Last year, more than two million Australians lost a combined total of $2.2 billion to card fraud, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

Card fraud involves the use of credit, debit, or EFTPOS card details to make purchases or withdraw cash without the account owner's permission.

But it can also happen "without your card ever leaving your wallet", according to experts.

Here are some of the more common types of card fraud, according to the experts, including their advice on how to keep your money safe when making transactions.

What is card skimming?

Rebecca Pritchard, a senior financial planner from Melbourne/Naarm, says skimming is when a small device is illegally attached to an ATM or payment terminal to capture your card's data when you swipe or insert it.

"A tiny camera or overlay keypad often captures your PIN at the same time," she says.

What is lifestyle creep and how to avoid it If you tend to splurge on more indulgences any time you receive a pay rise, you may be suffering from lifestyle creep — and it could have a longstanding effect on your finances.

"It's a bit old school now; most fraud has moved online. But it still happens, particularly at standalone ATMs and petrol stations."

Chris Sheehan, the executive for group investigations at the National Australia Bank, recommends always inspecting card readers at ATMs before using them — particularly f you see anything loose, crooked or damaged.

"Use the ATM's contactless card reader when available; this doesn't require you to insert your card into a card reader. And shield the keypad at the ATM so no-one can see you enter your PIN," he says.

Other common card fraud methods

Mr Sheehan says the most common card fraud reported to NAB occurs after a physical card is lost, or it has been stolen in the mail.

"Particularly blocks of townhouses or apartments where they've got lots of letterboxes outside," he says.

"Thieves will go and raid those for letters from banks that have got credit cards or debit cards in them."

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) says card fraud can also happen through:

Phishing scams: where criminals pretend to be your bank, a business or government agency and trick you into handing over card details, PINs or security codes

where criminals pretend to be your bank, a business or government agency and trick you into handing over card details, PINs or security codes Data breaches or insecure websites: if card details are entered into an unsafe website or shared over public wi-fi

if card details are entered into an unsafe website or shared over public wi-fi Account takeovers: where scammers gain access to online banking or shopping accounts and make unauthorised purchases or transfers

What are the best ways to protect your cards?

The ABS report found most victims didn't realise their card or account had been used fraudulently until they were contacted by their bank.

"Monitor your accounts regularly rather than waiting for your statement," Ms Pritchard says.

" Fraudsters often test with a small transaction first. "

Financial planner Rebecca Pritchard recommends regular checks of your bank account transactions. (Supplied)

Mr Sheehan also recommends using payment apps on your phone rather than a physical card.

"Using your mobile wallet, you get additional layers of security," he says.

"So, for example, with Apple Pay, you've got facial biometrics or sometimes fingerprint biometrics. It doesn't expose the card details to the merchant."

ASIC also recommends:

Keeping your PIN and passwords secret

Being cautious of unexpected calls, texts or emails asking for card or banking details

Setting up transaction notifications and transaction limits through your banking app

Considering overseas payment restrictions on your accounts

Contacting your bank immediately if your card is lost, stolen or you notice suspicious activity. Lock your card via your banking app or online banking portal

Using secure websites when shopping online (look for "https" and the lock symbol in the address bar) and avoid public wi-fi for banking

Keeping your contact details up to date so your bank can reach you quickly if something looks wrong

Measures like these "are designed to limit losses and help banks act quickly if fraud occurs," an ASIC spokesperson says.

Reimbursement 'not guaranteed'

ASIC says under the ePayments Code, banks must investigate unauthorised transactions, but "timing and consumer behaviour matter".

"Your first call should be your bank. The faster you act, the better your chances," Ms Pritchard says.

"The ABS data shows three in four people who experienced card fraud were fully reimbursed by their bank or card issuer, which sounds reassuring until you realise that still leaves one in four people out of pocket."

And if a debit or credit card is used without the customer's permission, "we will generally refund those unauthorised transactions", Mr Sheehan says.

He recommends reporting card fraud to your bank straight away.

"Number one, we want to stop the fraud from happening," he says.

"But secondly, the longer you leave it, the more difficult it might be to recover the evidence of what's actually occurred."

World.title: The moment Andy Lee feared exploits with Hamish Blake had gone too far
World.content:
For more than two decades, Andy Lee and Hamish Blake have been lovable larrikins making us laugh on their adventures both here and abroad.

But Lee said there were times they pushed their comedy, and their bodies, too far.

In fact, in one incident, Lee said he genuinely feared for Blake's life.

The affable pair had travelled to Bosnia, for their 'Gap Year' series, to jump 25 metres from a bridge in Mostar.

After seeking the advice of a local jumper, it was decided Lee would be the first to make the leap.

"I'm not particularly scared of heights, [but] Hamish is," Lee told ABC iview's The Assembly.

Lee said the jump left him "completely winded" and with "every vertebrae in his back" bruised.

"It was extremely painful," he said.

" I got to the edge of the river and I told the cameraman, 'Tell him not to jump, tell him not to jump, tell him not to jump'. "

But Blake had already stepped over the rail, and was teetering on the edge.

"That's the time I felt the most scared for my friend and thought, 'We shouldn't be doing this'. So, please no-one go and do that."

For their 2012 TV show, Lee organised for he and Blake to jump off the Mostar Bridge in Bosnia. (Supplied: Hamish & Andy's Euro Gap Year)

Blake emerged from the jump unscathed, but Lee hadn't been so lucky two years earlier, when another of their trademark shenanigans led to major dental surgery.

"These two front teeth are fake," Lee said.

"I smashed them playing ice hockey with Hamish. I had to have them taken out and I've got a titanium tooth.

"They had to rebuild my jawline with cow bone."

'Do I exist without Hamish?'

Not even the loss of two front teeth tested the pair's friendship, with Lee full of praise for his comedy partner and best mate.

"He's so funny," Lee said.

"But beyond funniness, he's an amazing friend."

Lee said he always knew an adventure was in store when he spent time with Blake.

"When you catch up with Hame, you know something fun is going to happen," he said.

"I'm not saying that every friend has to be this outrageous, funny, adventurous person, but that's what draws me to Hame, and I just never get sick of him."

Blake and Lee, pictured in 2010, started performing on radio together in the early 2000s. (Getty: Matt Jelonek)

But like the best of us, Lee said Blake had his fair share of foibles.

"Hamish, as he put it himself, is 'fast and loose'. So he's very unpredictable at times, which makes him a lot of fun, but also you can be left with, 'Where is he? Is he coming?'" Lee said.

Like the time Lee was waiting at a cafe for Blake to arrive. After 15 minutes with no word from Blake, Lee gave him a friendly check-in call.

"He picked up the phone and says, 'Do you think we need a radar gun? I'm at the cricket shop — it could be fun to see how fast we're bowling,'" Lee said.

"Neither of us really play cricket, but this is the impulsive nature of Hame — he gets on the scent of something like an excitable dog hound and off he goes.

"It normally follows fun and adventure … which I've benefited from many, many times."

Loading...

Lee and Blake have always encouraged each other to pursue opportunities individually, which they each could learn from and share with the other.

But Lee's candid about the self-doubt he's felt at times when taking on solo projects, sometimes worrying, "Do I exist without Hamish?"

"I'd be lying to say I wasn't nervous when I went out on my own," he said.

"When we are doing something so strong together — and I think the world of the way he performs — 'If I'm without him, what am I? Am I good enough?'" Lee said.

"Hamish is a safety blanket. I have to work much harder when I am not around him."

The secret to winning at life

After their long working relationship, comparisons between Blake and Lee are inevitable.

But when asked who's "winning at life", Lee was quick to claim that he was.

"I'm absolutely content with my fiancee and trying to build a house with my dog," he said.

Lee is enjoing life with fiancee Rebecca Harding, and their dog Henri, as they restore an abandoned Victorian-era manor. (Instagram: @andytomlee)

While Lee understands the "power of money", he doesn't see it as the best measure of success — or happiness.

"I've got a friend of mine who just works nine to five labouring. [He] clocks off, goes to the pub, hangs out with friends and has the best time and doesn't worry about work.

"I actually think he's the most successful, because it's exactly what he wants to do and he feels really content.

"So if you're content with what you're doing, I think you're winning life."

Stream all episodes of The Assembly on ABC iview or watch Sundays on ABC TV at 8:30pm.

World.title: Trump calls for Jimmy Kimmel to be fired over ‘expectant widow’ joke
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaMelania Trump Trump calls for Jimmy Kimmel to be fired over ‘expectant widow’ joke Sarah McPhee Updated April 28, 2026 — 3:59am ,first published 2:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

US President Donald Trump has called for Jimmy Kimmel to be fired after the late-night talk show host remarked first lady Melania Trump had the glow of an “expectant widow” in a monologue delivered before an assassination attempt in Washington. “I appreciate that so many people are incensed by Kimmel’s despicable call to violence, and normally would not be responsive to anything that he said but, this is something far beyond the pale,” Trump said on Truth Social on Monday US time (Tuesday AEST). “Jimmy Kimmel should be immediately fired by Disney and ABC.” First lady Melania Trump at a press conference after the shooting. AP Trump’s post followed one made by his wife, Melania Trump, who wrote on X: “Enough is enough. It is time for ABC to take a stand. How many times will ABC’s leadership enable Kimmel’s atrocious behaviour at the expense of our community.” “His monologue about my family isn’t comedy,” she added, describing it as “hateful and violent rhetoric”.





In a press briefing on Monday US time (Tuesday AEST), White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Kimmel had “disgustingly” called the first lady an “expectant widow”. “Who in their right mind says a wife would be glowing over the potential murder of her beloved husband? And having experienced what I did with the first lady on Saturday night, I can tell you that she was anything but that,” she said. Leavitt was seated at a long table at the dinner alongside the Trumps when the chaos erupted. Loading Alleged shooter Cole Allen is accused of sprinting through a checkpoint and firing at Secret Service agents, wounding one, before he was arrested. He has been charged with a number of offences including the alleged attempt assassination of the president.



The first lady later appeared alongside her husband as he briefed reporters at the White House on Saturday night (US time). He described the incident as “a rather traumatic experience” for her. Asked during an interview with CBS’ 60 Minutes on Sunday whether his wife had been scared, the president said: “I don’t want to say, and people don’t like having it said that they were scared, but certainly, I mean, who wouldn’t be when you have a situation like that?” US first lady Melania Trump and Donald Trump at the dinner before chaos erupted. Bloomberg In September, the head of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) pressured broadcasters to take Kimmel off the air. ABC briefly suspended Kimmel’s show that month over comments he made about the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. Hours before the suspension, FCC head Brendan Carr warned that local broadcasters who aired Kimmel could face fines or loss of licenses and said “it’s time for them to step up”. His comments garnered pushback from the entertainment industry and politicians on both sides of the aisle, including Republican Senator Ted Cruz, who likened his threats to that of an organised crime boss.



In September, Sinclair and Nexstar Media Group briefly took Kimmel’s show off the air on their 70 ABC-affiliated stations covering nearly a quarter of US households. Carr wants to make it easier for local broadcasters to preempt national programming. Related Article Updated

Trump's America ‘Friendly Federal Assassin’: Alleged shooter’s manifesto says he was targeting Trump officials In November, Trump criticised an ABC News correspondent for asking Saudi Arabia’s crown prince about the 2018 killing of a Washington Post columnist and suggested the commission should move to revoke the broadcast licenses of Disney-owned ABC stations. with Reuters, Bloomberg Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: OK Millennial: This is why young Australians will prosper like their parents
World.content:
PoliticsFederalFederal budget OK Millennial: This is why young Australians will prosper like their parents Shane Wright April 28, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Young Australians are likely to eventually prosper as well as their parents, research into the income battle between the generations has found, but they will struggle in their 30s as they contend with imposts their parents never had to face. Compiled by independent think tank the e61 Institute, the research suggests younger people with rich parents who are sitting on large bequests will do best in coming years, with inheritances likely to be the biggest driver of inequality between Millennials. Research shows young Australians will eventually be no worse off than their parents – though they face headwinds. Oscar Colman Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese have both said that next month’s federal budget will tackle “intergenerational equity” in a direct pitch to people in their 20s, 30s and 40s who believe the economy and housing markets are working against them. Current capital gains tax and negative gearing settings, which critics argue benefit older Australians while putting upward pressure on rents and house prices, are expected to be overhauled in the May 12 budget.



But e61 principal economist Jack Buckley said that while intergenerational inequity may be a key theme of the budget, it ignored how the mix of income wealth and taxes changed as people aged. Related Article Opinion

Federal budget The PM’s about to offer selfish Boomers like me a chance at redemption Peter Hartcher Political and international editor He said the average inflation-adjusted income for a 35-year-old in 2023 was about $90,000, almost 80 per cent higher than the average 35-year-old in the late 1980s. Median household wealth, however, was about the same today, at $380,000, as it was for earlier generations at the same age. According to Buckley, older Australians had largely benefited from a large run-up in the value of assets such as housing, which were also lightly taxed. “The truth is that younger Australians are unlikely to be worse off than their parents over their lifetimes,” he said. “Income growth has slowed early in their careers, partly because young people are spending longer in education, but they are likely to see stronger earnings growth later in life.”



According to the e61 research, people in their 30s were being squeezed the most by policies not faced by their parents that will ultimately deliver them a boost in income in their later years. More years in education, large HELP and HECS repayments and the 12 per cent superannuation guarantee all eat into the current incomes of people just as they try to save for a home and start a family. This meant income growth for younger Australians was slower than for previous generations. But over time, higher wages plus the superannuation system would increase their wealth to a level on par with their parents. Buckley said the run-up in house prices that had increased the wealth of older Australians who were now sitting on an “inheritance boom” would contribute to a large jump in inequality within generations rather than between the generations. “Older Australians are sitting on a windfall from rising asset prices, and most of that wealth will be passed down unevenly through inheritance,” he said.



“That inheritance boom will increase inequality within a generation in a way that’s far more consequential than any gap between generations.” The research does confirm that older Australians are, in some ways, doing better than younger generations. The post-tax income of over 60s is now 95 per cent of that of 18- to 60-year-olds. In the 1990s, it was about 61 per cent. Housing costs remain a dividing line between young and old Australians. Audrey Richardson Over that same period, the share of tax paid by over 60s has not increased. Buckley said reforms such as an inheritance tax, which was canvassed by the Henry tax review of 2010, could encourage older people to tap their wealth rather than building up inheritances, but they were likely to be politically unpalatable.



Support for changing capital gains tax in next week’s budget remains high among a large group of organisations, from the ACTU to the St Vincent de Paul Society charity. Related Article Exclusive

Federal budget CGT like it’s 1999: Chalmers leans towards scrapping Howard-Costello tax discount This masthead revealed earlier this month that the government is likely to ditch the current 50 per cent concession on the tax, introduced by the Howard government in 1999, and return to the original inflation-adjustment system put in place when the Hawke government started the CGT in the mid-1980s. Any change to the CGT concession, which applies to assets including shares and cryptocurrency, is expected to be grandfathered – only apply to new acquisitions – rather than made retrospective. Westpac chief economist Luci Ellis warned that while a change to the CGT may increase government revenues, this was not guaranteed as much hinged on how fast asset prices climb.



She cautioned that just “tweaking” the tax system may not be the only or best way to deal with an issue like a shortfall in government revenue or housing affordability. “Global economic and geopolitical developments pose challenges, while new technology and an expanding, ageing workforce create opportunities,” she said. “We should not assume that tweaking the tax system is the answer to every issue.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Compulsory safety training ramps up online to tackle childcare abuse crisis
World.content:
PoliticsFederalChildcare Compulsory safety training ramps up online to tackle childcare abuse crisis Brittany Busch April 27, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Two-thirds of childcare workers have completed new mandatory child safety training as the government cracks down on the sector following a spate of abuse cases in centres around the country. A third of workers yet to complete the training will have to do so before the six-month deadline expires in late August. Since the government made the online safety course compulsory as part of a $226 million package to bolster child safety, more than 180,000 of an estimated 270,000 sector workers have fulfilled the requirement. Minister for Education Jason Clare said the speed of the uptake showed how much educators cared about child safety. Kate Geraghty The sector was plunged into crisis after a slew of allegations against workers abusing children in their care was revealed, including in Melbourne, where alleged paedophile Joshua Brown was accused of sexually abusing eight toddlers and babies and contaminating children’s food with bodily fluids. In Sydney, it was revealed childcare worker David James, accused of abusing 10 children, had continued to work after his behaviour was reported to police. The Coalition has identified childcare – which costs the federal budget almost $16 billion each year – as a key policy battleground as parents say their confidence in the sector has faltered. The opposition is considering alternatives to centre-based care such as vouchers for nannies, while the prime minister aspires to a legacy of universal childcare – meaning accessible and affordable care for all children.



Education Minister Jason Clare said the speed with which the training has been taken up showed how much educators cared about child safety. Related Article Melbourne childcare crisis Daycare linked to sex abuse allegations shut down over serious child safety failures “They’ve been given six months to complete new safety training. The majority of them have done it in two months,” he said, adding staff were the best protection asset against abuse. “It tells you a lot about how much they care about and want to protect our kids.” Providers can claim a subsidy if they close a centre in the evening for staff to complete the training, for which up to $40 million has been committed annually from the child care subsidy budget. Workers must provide a completion certificate to their employers, and company directors and management are also required to participate.



The two-hour online training – developed by the Australian Centre for Child Protection – uses videos and multimedia to teach workers about child safety and how to identify abuse and neglect. It builds on a patchwork of existing training requirements to create a standardised national course. Related Article Childcare Coalition pushes for powers to more easily sack childcare workers Topics covered include how to develop child-safe policies and procedures and how to recognise grooming behaviours, such as an adult praising one child as being more mature or special than others. World.title: Trump calls for Jimmy Kimmel to be fired over ‘expectant widow’ joke
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaMelania Trump Trump calls for Jimmy Kimmel to be fired over ‘expectant widow’ joke Sarah McPhee Updated April 28, 2026 — 3:59am ,first published 2:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

US President Donald Trump has called for Jimmy Kimmel to be fired after the late-night talk show host remarked first lady Melania Trump had the glow of an “expectant widow” in a monologue delivered before an assassination attempt in Washington. “I appreciate that so many people are incensed by Kimmel’s despicable call to violence, and normally would not be responsive to anything that he said but, this is something far beyond the pale,” Trump said on Truth Social on Monday US time (Tuesday AEST). “Jimmy Kimmel should be immediately fired by Disney and ABC.” First lady Melania Trump at a press conference after the shooting. AP Trump’s post followed one made by his wife, Melania Trump, who wrote on X: “Enough is enough. It is time for ABC to take a stand. How many times will ABC’s leadership enable Kimmel’s atrocious behaviour at the expense of our community.” “His monologue about my family isn’t comedy,” she added, describing it as “hateful and violent rhetoric”.





In a press briefing on Monday US time (Tuesday AEST), White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Kimmel had “disgustingly” called the first lady an “expectant widow”. “Who in their right mind says a wife would be glowing over the potential murder of her beloved husband? And having experienced what I did with the first lady on Saturday night, I can tell you that she was anything but that,” she said. Leavitt was seated at a long table at the dinner alongside the Trumps when the chaos erupted. Loading Alleged shooter Cole Allen is accused of sprinting through a checkpoint and firing at Secret Service agents, wounding one, before he was arrested. He has been charged with a number of offences including the alleged attempt assassination of the president.



The first lady later appeared alongside her husband as he briefed reporters at the White House on Saturday night (US time). He described the incident as “a rather traumatic experience” for her. Asked during an interview with CBS’ 60 Minutes on Sunday whether his wife had been scared, the president said: “I don’t want to say, and people don’t like having it said that they were scared, but certainly, I mean, who wouldn’t be when you have a situation like that?” US first lady Melania Trump and Donald Trump at the dinner before chaos erupted. Bloomberg In September, the head of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) pressured broadcasters to take Kimmel off the air. ABC briefly suspended Kimmel’s show that month over comments he made about the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. Hours before the suspension, FCC head Brendan Carr warned that local broadcasters who aired Kimmel could face fines or loss of licenses and said “it’s time for them to step up”. His comments garnered pushback from the entertainment industry and politicians on both sides of the aisle, including Republican Senator Ted Cruz, who likened his threats to that of an organised crime boss.



In September, Sinclair and Nexstar Media Group briefly took Kimmel’s show off the air on their 70 ABC-affiliated stations covering nearly a quarter of US households. Carr wants to make it easier for local broadcasters to preempt national programming. Related Article Updated

Trump's America ‘Friendly Federal Assassin’: Alleged shooter’s manifesto says he was targeting Trump officials In November, Trump criticised an ABC News correspondent for asking Saudi Arabia’s crown prince about the 2018 killing of a Washington Post columnist and suggested the commission should move to revoke the broadcast licenses of Disney-owned ABC stations. with Reuters, Bloomberg Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: OK Millennial: This is why young Australians will prosper like their parents
World.content:
PoliticsFederalFederal budget OK Millennial: This is why young Australians will prosper like their parents Shane Wright April 28, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Young Australians are likely to eventually prosper as well as their parents, research into the income battle between the generations has found, but they will struggle in their 30s as they contend with imposts their parents never had to face. Compiled by independent think tank the e61 Institute, the research suggests younger people with rich parents who are sitting on large bequests will do best in coming years, with inheritances likely to be the biggest driver of inequality between Millennials. Research shows young Australians will eventually be no worse off than their parents – though they face headwinds. Oscar Colman Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese have both said that next month’s federal budget will tackle “intergenerational equity” in a direct pitch to people in their 20s, 30s and 40s who believe the economy and housing markets are working against them. Current capital gains tax and negative gearing settings, which critics argue benefit older Australians while putting upward pressure on rents and house prices, are expected to be overhauled in the May 12 budget.



But e61 principal economist Jack Buckley said that while intergenerational inequity may be a key theme of the budget, it ignored how the mix of income wealth and taxes changed as people aged. Related Article Opinion

Federal budget The PM’s about to offer selfish Boomers like me a chance at redemption Peter Hartcher Political and international editor He said the average inflation-adjusted income for a 35-year-old in 2023 was about $90,000, almost 80 per cent higher than the average 35-year-old in the late 1980s. Median household wealth, however, was about the same today, at $380,000, as it was for earlier generations at the same age. According to Buckley, older Australians had largely benefited from a large run-up in the value of assets such as housing, which were also lightly taxed. “The truth is that younger Australians are unlikely to be worse off than their parents over their lifetimes,” he said. “Income growth has slowed early in their careers, partly because young people are spending longer in education, but they are likely to see stronger earnings growth later in life.”



According to the e61 research, people in their 30s were being squeezed the most by policies not faced by their parents that will ultimately deliver them a boost in income in their later years. More years in education, large HELP and HECS repayments and the 12 per cent superannuation guarantee all eat into the current incomes of people just as they try to save for a home and start a family. This meant income growth for younger Australians was slower than for previous generations. But over time, higher wages plus the superannuation system would increase their wealth to a level on par with their parents. Buckley said the run-up in house prices that had increased the wealth of older Australians who were now sitting on an “inheritance boom” would contribute to a large jump in inequality within generations rather than between the generations. “Older Australians are sitting on a windfall from rising asset prices, and most of that wealth will be passed down unevenly through inheritance,” he said.



“That inheritance boom will increase inequality within a generation in a way that’s far more consequential than any gap between generations.” The research does confirm that older Australians are, in some ways, doing better than younger generations. The post-tax income of over 60s is now 95 per cent of that of 18- to 60-year-olds. In the 1990s, it was about 61 per cent. Housing costs remain a dividing line between young and old Australians. Audrey Richardson Over that same period, the share of tax paid by over 60s has not increased. Buckley said reforms such as an inheritance tax, which was canvassed by the Henry tax review of 2010, could encourage older people to tap their wealth rather than building up inheritances, but they were likely to be politically unpalatable.



Support for changing capital gains tax in next week’s budget remains high among a large group of organisations, from the ACTU to the St Vincent de Paul Society charity. Related Article Exclusive

Federal budget CGT like it’s 1999: Chalmers leans towards scrapping Howard-Costello tax discount This masthead revealed earlier this month that the government is likely to ditch the current 50 per cent concession on the tax, introduced by the Howard government in 1999, and return to the original inflation-adjustment system put in place when the Hawke government started the CGT in the mid-1980s. Any change to the CGT concession, which applies to assets including shares and cryptocurrency, is expected to be grandfathered – only apply to new acquisitions – rather than made retrospective. Westpac chief economist Luci Ellis warned that while a change to the CGT may increase government revenues, this was not guaranteed as much hinged on how fast asset prices climb.



She cautioned that just “tweaking” the tax system may not be the only or best way to deal with an issue like a shortfall in government revenue or housing affordability. “Global economic and geopolitical developments pose challenges, while new technology and an expanding, ageing workforce create opportunities,” she said. “We should not assume that tweaking the tax system is the answer to every issue.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis.
